title: Mind your manners? Demand, not register, is what moves an LLM agent
description:
A widely-discussed result reports that impolite prompts outperform polite ones on multiple-choice questions. That literature is single-turn; deployed systems are agents. We put a coding agent on SpreadsheetBench and varied the social register of a single 28-token interjection delivered mid-task. Every interjection is length-matched and opens with the same stem, so being interrupted does not covary with what the interruption says.

Across six mid-task runs on two models from different labs (9,850 scheduled trajectories, 6,616 in the primary analysis), persistence tracks implied task demand more closely than social register. An affect-free "please continue working" reproduces the increase in turns, while a length-matched insult carrying no demand does not lengthen trajectories (−0.08 turns, 95% CI [−0.40, +0.24] at the ten-turn budget). Across six register arms the ordering follows our demand coding rather than politeness, with polite and hostile arms on both sides; blinded raters dispute that coding for one arm, so we report an ordering, not a clean dichotomy. Register acts on its own in one direction only: praise carrying no task reference shortens trajectories, and so does a note saying no further notes will follow (−1.44 turns). We leave the mechanism of these shortening effects open. Per-turn regrading shows that on the main model 56–93% of each clear turn-count effect is steps after which the graded range did not change. No accuracy effect survives correction or replication, and pooled accuracy contrasts are equivalent within a ±4-point bound taken from the tone literature (an exploratory analysis, not pre-registered).

The practical implication is altered control flow rather than measured lost correctness: a status note appended to an agent's tool output changed when it stopped, without instructing it to stop.
